lesson_title: One Question That Sorts Every Change in Chemistry
hook_text: Your fizzy drink and a fizzing tablet make the SAME bubbles — and chemistry says they are opposites.
clip_script: Two glasses, both fizzing. Glass one: a cold drink you just opened. Glass two: a headache tablet dropped in water. Identical bubbles — opposite verdicts. The whole of chemistry sorts every change with one question: is a new substance formed? The cold drink's gas was already in there, dissolved under pressure at the factory. Open the cap and it simply escapes — nothing new was made. Physical. The tablet is a factory in miniature: its ingredients react the moment water lets them meet, manufacturing carbon dioxide that never existed in the tablet as gas. New substance. Chemical. Same trick everywhere. Chocolate melts in your pocket — still chocolate — physical. A match burns — smoke and a black stump, never a match again — chemical. Sugar dissolving in tea, physical; sugar browning into caramel in the pan, chemical — cooled caramel is not sugar. And nothing is ever lost either way: burnt steel wool actually gets HEAVIER, because the iron borrows oxygen from the air. Atoms regroup; they never vanish. One question — is there a new substance? Ask it, and you can classify any change in the universe.
visual_style: Split screen of two fizzing glasses under moody kitchen light, labels PHYSICAL and CHEMICAL sliding onto each side; quick macro cuts — chocolate softening, a match flaring to black, sugar darkening to caramel, steel wool glowing and tipping a balance scale downward.
mood: Playful myth-bust — two identical-looking events pulled apart by one sharp question.
pacing: Fast twin-glass open, snappy verdict swaps on each example, slowing for the steel-wool reveal and the one-question punchline.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and take the one deciding question into every exam.
